english: Some others are secretly introducing another doctrine, who have become disciples of one Noetus, who was a native of Smyrna, (and) lived not very long ago. This person was greatly puffed up and inflated with pride, being inspired by the conceit of a strange spirit. He alleged that Christ was the Father Himself, and that the Father Himself was born, and suffered, and died.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5 section heading '[Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond.]', archive.org OCR line 23751)

limits: Opponent's claim in the author's own voice; it is the thing being refuted, not Hippolytus's doctrine. Noetus is only one name in the chapter (Migne PG 10 note: Epiphanius places Noetus in Ephesus, not Smyrna; a variant to report).

english: Ye see what pride of heart and what a strange inflated spirit had insinuated themselves into him. From his other actions, then, the proof is already given us that he spoke not with a pure spirit; for he who blasphemes against the Holy Ghost is cast out from the holy inheritance. He alleged that he was himself Moses, and that Aaron was his brother.

english: And the presbyters replied to him, “We too know in truth one God; we know Christ; we know that the Son suffered even as He suffered, and died even as He died, and rose again on the third day, and is at the right hand of the Father, and cometh to judge the living and the dead. And these things which we have learned we allege.”
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5 section heading '[Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond.]', archive.org OCR line 23751)

what_it_says: The presbyters' confession: one God, Christ, the Son who suffered, rose and is at the Father's right hand; no Holy Spirit is named here.
limits: The CCEL footnote says the words are the Symbol as in Irenaeus i.10, iii.4 and Tertullian, Adv. Prax. 2. Hippolytus's stress is that the SON suffered, not the Father. The confession names no Holy Spirit, so it is not a full triad. Unitarians will say it confesses one God 'the Father'.

english: And then they answer in this manner: “If therefore I acknowledge Christ to be God, He is the Father Himself, if He is indeed God; and Christ suffered, being Himself God; and consequently the Father suffered, for He was the Father Himself.” But the case stands not thus; for the Scriptures do not set forth the matter in this manner.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5 section heading '[Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond.]', archive.org OCR line 23751)

what_it_says: The Patripassian syllogism: Christ is God, so Christ is the Father; Christ suffered, so the Father suffered. Hippolytus rejects the inference.
limits: He rejects it with 'not so' and no argument yet; the Father/Son distinction is developed only later in the treatise (chs. 10-11 are outside this assignment). Note the wording 'Christ is God' is shared by Nicene and Noetian readers.

english: 3. In this way, then, they choose to set forth these things, and they make use only of one class of passages; just in the same one-sided manner that Theodotus employed when he sought to prove that Christ was a mere man. But neither has the one party nor the other understood the matter rightly, as the Scriptures themselves confute their senselessness, and attest the truth. See, brethren, what a rash and audacious dogma they have introduced, when they say without shame, the Father is Himself Christ, Himself the Son, Himself was born, Himself suffered, Himself raised Himself. But it is not so.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5 section heading '[Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond.]', archive.org OCR line 23751)

english: The proper way, therefore, to deal with the question is first of all to refute the interpretation put upon these passages by these men, and then to explain their real meaning. For it is right, in the first place, to expound the truth that the Father is one God, “of whom is every family,” “by whom are all things, of whom are all things, and we in Him.”
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5 section heading '[Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond.]', archive.org OCR line 23751)

english: Many other passages, or rather all of them, attest the truth. A man, therefore, even though he will it not, is compelled to acknowledge God the Father Almighty, and Christ Jesus the Son of God, who, being God, became man, to whom also the Father made all things subject, Himself excepted, and the Holy Spirit; and that these, therefore, are three.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5 section heading '[Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond.]', archive.org OCR line 23751)
edition: Lagarde, Teubner 1858 (archive.org hippolytiromani00lagagoog); ANF vol. 5, 1886 (CCEL text; archive.org 'Ante Nicene Fathers, Vol 5' for page numbers)
what_it_says: Scripture compels one to confess God the Father Almighty, Christ Jesus the Son of God who became man, and the Holy Spirit: 'these are truly three' (τρία).
limits: The clearest triadic sentence in the chapter. Note: the Holy Spirit is listed with the Father and Son as 'three' (τρία); the Son is 'God who became man', not named 'homoousios'. Greek here is 'θεὸν ἄνθρωπον γενόμενον' (ANF 'who, being God, became man'). Text as read on the Lagarde page image (p. 50).

greek: εἰ δὲ βούλεται μαθεῖν, πῶς εἷς θεὸς ἀποδείκνυται, γινωσκέτω ὅτι μία δύναμις τούτου, καὶ ὅσον μὲν κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν, εἷς ἐστι θεός, ὅσον δὲ κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομίαν, τριχῆς ἡ ἐπίδειξις, ὡς ὕστερον ἀποδειχθήσεται, ἀποδιδόντων ἡμῶν περὶ ἀληθείας λόγον.

english: But if he desires to learn how it is shown still that there is one God, let him know that His power is one. As far as regards the power, therefore, God is one. But as far as regards the economy there is a threefold manifestation, as shall be proved afterwards when we give account of the true doctrine.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5 section heading '[Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond.]', archive.org OCR line 23751)
edition: Lagarde, Teubner 1858 (archive.org hippolytiromani00lagagoog); ANF vol. 5, 1886 (CCEL text; archive.org 'Ante Nicene Fathers, Vol 5' for page numbers)
what_it_says: God is one by power (δύναμις), but by economy the manifestation is threefold; the threefold account is promised for later.
limits: Hippolytus does not finish the promised account in this treatise's chapters 1-8. The 'one power / threefold economy' distinction is the key tool for 'modalist vs Trinitarian' readings. The phrase 'τριχῆς ἡ ἐπίδειξις' is not repeated here.

greek: εἷς γὰρ θεός ἐστιν ᾧ δεῖ πιστεύειν, ἀλλ' ἀγέννητος, ἀπαθής, ἀθάνατος, πάντα ποιῶν ἃ θέλει, καθὼς θέλει, ὅτε θέλει. τί οὖν πρὸς ταῦτα τολμήσει Νόητος μὴ νοῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν;

english: For there is one God in whom we must believe, but unoriginated, impassible, immortal, doing all things as He wills, in the way He wills, and when He wills. What, then, will this Noetus, who knows nothing of the truth, dare to say to these things?
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5 section heading '[Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond.]', archive.org OCR line 23751)
edition: Lagarde, Teubner 1858 (archive.org hippolytiromani00lagagoog); ANF vol. 5, 1886 (CCEL text; archive.org 'Ante Nicene Fathers, Vol 5' for page numbers)
what_it_says: God is unoriginated (ἀγέννητος), impassible and immortal, doing all as he wills; this excludes the Noetian Father who suffers.
limits: 'Unoriginated' (ἀγέννητος) is the attribute Arians reserve for the Father alone; the chapter does not say the Son is 'originated' here. Impassibility (ἀπαθής) is the point against Noetus. Lagarde: 'ἀγέννητος' as printed; ANF footnote notes the Νόητος/νοῶν pun.
